questions.q: Friction is a force that resists the motion of one surface across another. In which direction does the frictional force act relative to the surface interface?
options: Perpendicular to the surface interface, like the normal reaction force
Parallel to the surface interface, while the normal reaction force acts perpendicularly to it
In the same direction as the applied force that pushes the surfaces
Always vertically downwards, in the direction of the weight
questions.explanation: The frictional force Ff acts parallel to the surface interface, whereas the normal reaction force acts perpendicularly to the interface. Friction resists the relative motion of one surface across another, arising from the irregularities and bonds between the two surfaces in contact.

questions.q: The frictional force Ff is directly proportional to the normal reaction force and the coefficient of friction (μ), so Ff = μR. What is true of the coefficient of friction?
options: It is measured in newtons and is always greater than 1
It has no units, being the ratio of the frictional force to the normal reaction force, and usually has a value less than 1
It equals the normal reaction force divided by the weight of the object
It depends only on the contact area between the two surfaces
questions.explanation: Because Ff = μR, the coefficient of friction μ is the ratio of the frictional force to the normal reaction force, so it has no units. It usually has a value less than 1 and varies widely depending on the combination of surfaces in contact, such as aluminium sliding across wood versus aluminium sliding across ice.

questions.q: A 4 kg box is placed on a level piece of carpet with a coefficient of static friction μs = 0.5. Calculate the minimum force (the limiting friction) required to start the box moving. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
working: On level ground the normal reaction balances the weight: \(R = mg\)
At least 19.6 N must be applied to start the box moving.
questions.explanation: On a level surface the normal reaction force R equals the weight mg = 39.2 N. The limiting friction is the maximum static friction, μs R = 0.5 × 39.2 = 19.6 N, so the applied force must exceed this to overcome static friction and start the box moving.

questions.q: A car of mass 1600 kg rolls down a road inclined at 15° to the horizontal at constant speed, with air resistance negligible. Because the net force is zero, the road friction equals the component of the weight down the slope. Determine the magnitude of the road friction. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
working: The weight is resolved into a component down the slope \(W_{//}\) and one perpendicular to it \(W_\perp\).
\(W_\perp\) is balanced by the normal reaction force; the road friction balances \(W_{//}\).
questions.explanation: Because the car rolls at constant speed the net force is zero, so the road friction must equal the component of the weight down the slope, W// = mg sin 15° ≈ 4100 N. The perpendicular component W⊥ = mg cos 15° is balanced separately by the normal reaction force.

questions.q: When the weight of a car on a slope is resolved into components parallel and perpendicular to the road surface, which statement is correct?
options: The normal reaction force is balanced by the component of the weight parallel to the surface

The normal reaction force is balanced by the component of the weight perpendicular to the surface, and the net force is the vector sum of the parallel weight component with road friction and air resistance
The net force has a large component perpendicular to the road surface, pushing the car off the slope
The full weight presses into the surface, so the normal reaction force equals the weight mg
questions.explanation: The normal reaction force is balanced by the component of the weight that is perpendicular to the surface, so the net force has no component perpendicular to the slope. The net force is the vector sum of the component of weight parallel to the surface together with road friction and air resistance, and it points down the slope, so the car accelerates down the slope.

questions.q: From memory, distinguish static friction, sliding friction and rolling friction, and state what is meant by the 'limiting friction'.
keyPoints: Static friction is the frictional force that must be overcome to start one surface moving across another; it grows to match the applied force up to a maximum value called the limiting friction.
Sliding friction takes effect once the static friction has been overcome and the materials are actually moving past each other; it is weaker than static friction in magnitude.
Rolling friction resists the motion of one surface rolling across another (such as a wheel on a road) and is much smaller than either static or sliding friction.
questions.explanation: If you recalled that static friction rises to the limiting friction before sliding begins, that sliding friction is weaker than static friction, and that rolling friction is the smallest of the three, grade yourself Good or Easy. The value of the limiting friction depends on the nature of the two surfaces in contact and the normal reaction force.

questions.q: A downhill skier with a mass of 60 kg is moving in a straight line down a slope inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Calculate the magnitude of the component of the skier's weight that is parallel to the slope. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
working: The component of the weight parallel to the slope is \(W_{//} = mg\sin\theta\).
questions.explanation: The component of the skier's weight parallel to the slope is mg sin 30° = 60 × 9.8 × 0.5 = 294 N. This down-slope weight component drives the skier down the slope; any forces resisting the movement are subtracted from it to give the net force on the skier.

questions.q: On an inclined plane at angle θ, why is the normal force equal to mg cos θ rather than the full weight mg?
options: Because friction removes part of the weight before it reaches the surface
Because the surface only needs to balance the perpendicular component of the weight, mg cos θ, while the down-slope component mg sin θ is not supported by the surface
Because the normal force always equals exactly half the weight on any slope
Because an object's mass decreases when it is placed on a slope
questions.explanation: The block does not accelerate perpendicular to the surface, so the normal force balances only the perpendicular component of the weight, mg cos θ. The other part, mg sin θ, points along the slope and is what makes the block slide, so it is not supported by the surface. On flat ground θ = 0 and cos 0 = 1, so the normal force equals the full weight mg.

questions.q: From memory: how does the weight of a block resolve on an incline of angle θ, and what is the acceleration of a block sliding down a frictionless incline?
keyPoints: The weight resolves into a component mg sin θ down the slope and a component mg cos θ pressing into the slope — 'down-slope is sine' (steeper means more sliding, and sine grows toward 1 as θ approaches 90°).
The normal force equals mg cos θ, which is less than the full weight mg.
On a frictionless incline the only force along the slope is mg sin θ, so mg sin θ = ma and the mass cancels: a = g sin θ, independent of mass.
questions.explanation: If you recalled 'down-slope is sine, into-slope is cosine', that N = mg cos θ, and that a = g sin θ for a frictionless incline (mass cancels), grade yourself Good or Easy. The memory hook is that a steeper slope means more sliding, so the down-slope component must be the sine term.

questions.q: A block slides down a frictionless incline at angle θ. Which statement about its acceleration is correct?
options: The acceleration depends on the block's mass — a heavier block accelerates faster
The acceleration is g sin θ down the slope, independent of mass, because the mass cancels in mg sin θ = ma
The acceleration is g cos θ down the slope
The block does not accelerate, because the normal force balances the whole weight
questions.explanation: On a frictionless incline the only force along the slope is the down-slope weight component mg sin θ. Applying Newton's second law, mg sin θ = ma, the mass cancels, giving a = g sin θ. For example at θ = 30°, a = 9.8 × sin 30° = 4.9 m s⁻², independent of the block's mass.
